paper: OSTI 2574844 — Spencer et al., high-order GFD (generalized finite difference) method for the time-harmonic cold-plasma wave equation in toroidal geometry, Phys. Plasmas 32, 063902 (2025)
scope_note: Replication reproduced the convergence-order claim (C1, C2) against an analytic plane wave in a homogeneous problem. Open questions below concern parts of the paper NOT covered by that reduction, or genuinely open methodological questions about GFD for cold-plasma waves.

questions.q: Does the O(h^{m-1}) convergence rate observed on the homogeneous plane-wave test survive when the anisotropic cold-plasma dielectric tensor is turned on and a resonance layer (perpendicular ion cyclotron / lower-hybrid) crosses the interior of the domain, or does the rate drop toward first-order at the singular layer?
questions.basis: Our C2 test and the paper's Fig. 2 both use the homogeneous reduction so that a plane wave is an exact solution. The full physical problem the paper is motivating (ICRH/ECRH) has resonances where components of the dielectric tensor diverge; standard theory says convergence order in the neighborhood of a resonance typically degrades below the smooth-problem rate. The paper does not report a measured order for the resonance-crossing case.
next_steps: Extend test_C2 to use a smoothly varying anisotropic tensor with a controlled crossing of Re(epsilon) = 0 near the domain center; measure NRMSD order for m = 2, 3, 4.
Compare on-resonance vs off-resonance star-condition-number distributions.
Ask the authors whether they observed order reduction in their ICRH runs and, if so, whether star density was locally increased to compensate.

questions.q: How does the physics-informed point generator (monitor h(x,y) = h0 · lambda_min(x,y) from the local cold-plasma dispersion relation) actually perform relative to a naive uniform-density cloud once tensor anisotropy and mode conversion are present — i.e., is the resolution economy real, or is it dominated by the pollution effect at long propagation distances?
questions.basis: Claim C3 is algorithmic and was explicitly not tested in this replication. The paper describes the generator but does not quantify its wall-clock or NRMSD savings vs a uniform cloud on the same demo problem; without that comparison it is unclear whether the sophistication is what buys the reported qualitative fidelity in the ICRH/ECRH demos or whether uniform refinement would suffice.
next_steps: Implement a monitor-function point placer that mirrors the paper's Sec. IV description.
Run the plane-wave-in-varying-dielectric benchmark at fixed target NRMSD, with physics-informed vs uniform clouds; compare N_nodes and solve time.
Extend to a mode-conversion test case (fast → slow wave) and measure how well the generator resolves the short-wavelength component.

questions.q: The GFD star matrix is built with a TSVD-regularized Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and column scaling D_i2, but the paper does not publish a truncation-tolerance schedule; how sensitive is the reported convergence order to the SVD truncation cutoff and to the specific column-scaling definition, particularly for large stars (m = 4, ~41 nodes) where several singular values approach the floor?
questions.basis: Our own runs used the natural Moore–Penrose default and the observed orders match. But TSVD tolerance is a well-known lever in weighted-least-squares FD methods — too tight and you lose ill-conditioned but physically meaningful modes, too loose and the weights blow up. The paper's Table III specifies structure but not the numerical regularization schedule, so a legitimate reproduction ambiguity remains.
next_steps: Add a tolerance sweep to gfdm_core.gfd_weights (tolerance ∈ {1e-8, 1e-10, 1e-12, 1e-14}) and re-run test_C1/C2.
Report κ_i distributions and how many singular values are truncated per star.
Ask authors for their tolerance policy and whether it adapts per star.

questions.q: Do stars adjacent to the boundary — which necessarily have fewer neighbors on one side — silently degrade the interior convergence rate, and is this what causes the coarse-grid noise the paper attributes to 'irregular clouds' and the 'pollution effect'?
questions.basis: The paper reports noisy convergence on coarse clouds and attributes it to cloud regeneration + Helmholtz pollution. But an alternative (and complementary) explanation is boundary-star asymmetry: interior stars are near-symmetric, boundary stars are biased, and their weights leak into interior nodes through the assembled global operator. Neither the paper nor this replication separately measures interior-only versus full-domain NRMSD.
next_steps: Modify the C2 driver to compute NRMSD restricted to nodes at least R away from the boundary (R = star radius × 2), for varying R.
Plot interior-only convergence vs full-domain convergence at m = 2, 3, 4.
If the gap is large, propose a boundary-star enrichment strategy (ghost points, one-sided high-order stencils).

questions.q: Is the sparse direct solve (scipy spsolve / whatever direct solver the paper uses) actually scalable to the 3D toroidal problem sizes needed for real ICRH/ECRH design work, or does the dense-star bandwidth of the assembled 3N × 3N system force a switch to a preconditioned Krylov method — and if so, does the loss of exactness affect the observed convergence order?
questions.basis: The paper solves a 2D reduction directly. The natural next step (and the paper motivates it) is a full toroidal 3D solve; the star sizes 17/31/41 imply a global operator with hundreds of nonzeros per row and bandwidths that scale poorly with N. Direct solves become impractical; but Helmholtz problems with mixed-sign spectra are notoriously hard for iterative solvers, and any inexact solve can mask (or manufacture) a convergence order. Neither the paper nor our replication touches this.
next_steps: Estimate 3D operator memory and non-zero counts for realistic tokamak resolution (~10^6 nodes).
Run a benchmark comparing direct vs GMRES with ILU / shifted Laplacian preconditioners on the 2D BVP; measure convergence order under each solver.
Ask the authors what their planned 3D solver strategy is and whether they have measured order in the iterative-solve regime.
